warmup.q: A flow reads three lines of a delivery note at once and emits each item. The collector needs 30 ms to put each item away. You add .flowOn(io) before collect. What is the order of the read and stored lines now?
options: read 1, stored 1, read 2, stored 2, read 3, stored 3, the same as without flowOn
read 1, read 2, read 3, then stored 1, stored 2, stored 3
stored 1, stored 2, stored 3, then the reads
The flow throws "Flow invariant is violated"
warmup.why: With a different dispatcher, flowOn runs the reader in a second coroutine and puts a 64-slot channel between the two sides. The reader's emit now only puts the item into the channel, so it reads all three lines before the first 30 ms of putting away is done. The invariant error is for withContext around emit, not for flowOn.

opening:
The grocer's van has been. With the shopping comes a delivery note, one line per item, such as flour,2000,g, read by the old reader from Flow basics whose readLine holds its thread while it waits. Each line means an item to put away and write in the pantry book. Only one person may write in that book at a time, and it lives at the kitchen table. The reading is slow, waiting work, and it belongs in the back room, on another thread.

One line moves it: flowOn(io). The reading goes to the back room, the pantry book stays at the table, and the print order changes in a way that surprises people. The obvious alternative, wrapping the read and the emit in withContext(io), is the one the inspector refused in Inside flow { }.

In this lesson, we'll watch flowOn let the reader run ahead, build it by hand from a channel, count the rooms when a chain has several walls, and let several cooks share one hatch with channelFlow. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a delivery note to read in the back room and a pantry book that must stay at the table. flowOn builds the wall: the code above it runs in a second coroutine, a hatch with 64 spots sits between, and the collector never moves. Several walls make several rooms, and channelFlow lets several cooks share one hatch.

Now find each flowOn in your own code and read its chain from the bottom up. Check that nothing which must stay put, such as a client that isn't thread-safe, sits above it.

Next, we'll look at the shelf in the hatch. How many plates should it hold, and which plate is lost when it's full?

sections.h: Add flowOn and the reader runs ahead of the collector
sections.html:
Here is the delivery note as a flow. A dispatcher is the part of the coroutines library that decides which thread runs a coroutine. flowOn(io) asks for the code above it to run on io, here a dispatcher with one thread named io-thread. Putting an item away takes the collector 30 ms. Predict the order of the six lines:

Java
// Java equivalent: a reader thread puts items into a 64-slot BlockingQueue,
// and the main thread takes them out and stores them
BlockingQueue<String> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64);
new Thread(() -> { for (String item : items) put(hatch, item); put(hatch, END); }, "io-thread").start();
for (String item = hatch.take(); !item.equals(END); item = hatch.take()) {
    Thread.sleep(30);                // put it away and write it in the pantry book
    System.out.println("stored  " + item + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
}
Kotlin
deliveryItems()                      // prints "read <item> on <thread>", then emits the item
    .flowOn(io)
    .collect { item ->
        delay(30)                    // put it away and write it in the pantry book
        println("stored  $item on ${Thread.currentThread().name}")
    }

Without flowOn you get lesson 1's pattern: read, stored, read, stored, all on main. With it:

read    flour  on io-thread
read    eggs   on io-thread
read    milk   on io-thread
stored  flour  on main
stored  eggs   on main
stored  milk   on main

The reader ran ahead. It read all three lines before the first item was put away, so its emit calls returned without waiting for the collector. In lesson 1, emit couldn't return before the collector did. Something now sits between the two sides and holds values, and the two sides run on different threads. The Java twin prints the same six lines, and it shows what that something is: a queue.

Why not just wrap the read and the emit in withContext(io)? withContext runs one block of code in another context and comes back, as Dispatchers and the coroutine context showed. Lesson 2 showed what flow { } says to it here: "Flow invariant is violated". It also showed why. A hand-written raw Flow with no inspector ran its collector on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1. The collector runs inside emit, so an emit on an IO thread drags the collector onto that thread too.

That's a real bug, not a matter of style. The pantry book is not thread-safe: two threads writing in it at the same moment can mix up their lines, so all the writing must happen on one side. To move the reader and leave the collector alone, you have to break the call chain between them. That takes a second coroutine and a place to keep values in between, and we can build both from tools the coroutines track already gave us.

code.title: FlowOnOrder.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors val deliveryNote = listOf("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs", "milk,1000,ml") /** Reads the grocer's delivery note. Each line is read at once; it prints which thread read it. */ fun deliveryItems(): Flow<String> = flow { for (line in deliveryNote) { val item = line.substringBefore(",") println("read %-6s on %s".format(item, Thread.currentThread().name)) emit(item) } } fun main() = runBlocking { val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "io-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() println("=== plain, as in lesson 1") deliveryItems().collect { item -> delay(30) // put it away and write it in the pantry book println("stored %-6s on %s".format(item, Thread.currentThread().name)) } println("=== with .flowOn(io)") deliveryItems().flowOn(io).collect { item -> delay(30) println("stored %-6s on %s".format(item, Thread.currentThread().name)) } io.close() }

alt.title: FlowOnOrderJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowOnOrder.kt with flowOn: a reader thread puts items into a BlockingQueue // with 64 slots, and the main thread takes them out and stores them. That queue is the channel // that flowOn builds: the hatch in the wall. package workbench.flows.l03; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; public class FlowOnOrderJava { static final String END = "<end>"; // a queue can't be closed, so the reader sends an end marker public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { List<String> deliveryNote = List.of("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs", "milk,1000,ml"); BlockingQueue<String> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); Thread reader = new Thread(() -> { try { for (String line : deliveryNote) { String item = line.substring(0, line.indexOf(',')); System.out.printf("read %-6s on %s%n", item, Thread.currentThread().getName()); hatch.put(item); // blocks only when all 64 slots are full } hatch.put(END); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "io-thread"); reader.start(); for (String item = hatch.take(); !item.equals(END); item = hatch.take()) { Thread.sleep(30); // put it away and write it in the pantry book System.out.printf("stored %-6s on %s%n", item, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } reader.join(); } }

try.expect: Without flowOn, read and stored alternate on main. With it, the three reads come first on io-thread, then the three stores on main. With flowOn(CoroutineName("reader")) the order goes back to read, stored, read, stored, all on main: the dispatcher didn't change, so there is no second coroutine and no channel. The section on several walls comes back to this. The Java twin with a BlockingQueue prints the same six lines as the Kotlin version with flowOn(io).

sections.h: What flowOn builds: a wall with a hatch and a 64-spot shelf
sections.html:
The tools come from Channels, select and pipelines. A channel is a queue between coroutines: send waits when it is full, and receive waits when it is empty. produce starts a coroutine that sends into a new channel, and hands you the receiving end. With those two, flowOn takes eight lines:

Java
// Java equivalent: an executor for the upstream and a 64-slot queue in between
static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream)
        throws InterruptedException {
    BlockingQueue<Object> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64);
    executor.execute(() -> {
        upstream.accept(value -> put(hatch, value));     // the upstream's emit now means put
        put(hatch, END);
    });
    for (Object v = hatch.take(); v != END; v = hatch.take()) downstream.accept((T) v);
}
Kotlin
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)                     // produce is experimental in 1.11.0
fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow {
    coroutineScope {
        val hatch = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) {      // the second cook, behind the wall
            this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) }                 // the upstream's emit now means send
        }
        for (value in hatch) emit(value)                       // we stay in the collector's coroutine
    }
}

Read it as a picture, and the kitchen gets a wall. Across it runs a wall with a hatch in it, the hatch from Channels, select and pipelines, with a shelf that holds 64 plates. Behind the wall, a second cook, the produce coroutine, works on io and puts each plate on the shelf. In front, the original side takes plates off and hands them to the diner. Your emit calls now happen in the collector's own coroutine, so the inspector from lesson 2 has nothing to complain about. Nobody carries a plate through the wall by hand.

The real flowOn does the same, with one shortcut. flowOn(ctx) returns a ChannelFlowOperatorImpl. When it is collected, it compares contexts. If the dispatcher is the same as the collector's, it runs the upstream in place with the new context and builds no channel. If the dispatcher differs, it runs coroutineScope { collector.emitAll(produceImpl(this)) }. That produce collects the upstream into a SendingCollector, whose emit is channel.send(value). The channel's default capacity is Channel.BUFFERED, which is 64.

Two measurements show it. The first is a probe: the collector holds the first value and doesn't return, and we count how many emit calls return meanwhile. A plain flow gives 0. Both myFlowOn(io) and flowOn(io) give 65: 64 on the shelf and one in the diner's hands. Then the 66th send suspends, because the shelf is full. So flowOn doesn't remove backpressure. It moves it from "wait for the collector" to "wait for a free spot", and a slow collector still slows the reader down, 64 lines later.

The second is the collector's stack after flowOn(io), with repeated and helper frames trimmed:

    at HandMadeFlowOnKt$main$1$9.emit                                              <- your collector
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.FlowKt__ChannelsKt.emitAllImpl$FlowKt__ChannelsKt   <- the loop that empties the hatch
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.FlowKt__ChannelsKt.emitAll
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.internal.ChannelFlow$collect$2.invokeSuspend
    at kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScopeKt.coroutineScope
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.internal.ChannelFlow.collect
    at HandMadeFlowOnKt$main$1.invokeSuspend                                       <- main, calling collect

Your flow { } block is gone from it. It runs on another thread, in another coroutine, and only the loop that empties the hatch, emitAllImpl, calls your collector.

The hatch picture breaks in one place. A real hatch just sits in the wall. This one makes the cook behind the wall wait when the shelf is full, and when the diner stops collecting, the whole back room is cancelled.

flowOn moves the code above it behind a wall. The collector never moves.

One wall makes two rooms. Real chains sometimes have more than one flowOn, and that's where people lose track of who runs where.

Run it. Then find your flow { } block in the printed stack. Is it there?

code.title: HandMadeFlowOn.kt
code.html: @file:OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) package workbench.flows.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.produce import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** flowOn by hand: a second coroutine on [dispatcher] sends into a 64-slot channel, and we drain it. */ fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val hatch = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) { // the second cook, behind the wall this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) } // the upstream's emit now puts a plate in the hatch } for (value in hatch) emit(value) // we stay in the collector's coroutine } } /** How many emits return while the collector still holds the first value? */ suspend fun ahead(label: String, op: (Flow<Int>) -> Flow<Int>) = coroutineScope { val returned = AtomicInteger() val gate = CompletableDeferred<Unit>() var received = 0 val source = flow { for (i in 1..200) { emit(i); returned.set(i) } } val job = launch { op(source).collect { received++; if (received == 1) gate.await() } } delay(200) // let the producer run as far as it can val heldAt = returned.get() gate.complete(Unit) job.join() println("%-22s emits returned while the collector held item 1: %3d (received %d)".format(label, heldAt, received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "io-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() println("=== who runs where") flow { emit("flour"); println("emit flour returned on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } .myFlowOn(io) .collect { println("myFlowOn: collected $it on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } flow { emit("flour"); println("emit flour returned on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } .flowOn(io) .collect { println("flowOn: collected $it on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } println("=== how far ahead the producer gets") ahead("plain") { it } ahead("myFlowOn(io)") { it.myFlowOn(io) } ahead("flowOn(io)") { it.flowOn(io) } println("=== the collector's stack after flowOn(io)") flow { emit("flour") }.flowOn(io).collect { Thread.currentThread().stackTrace.drop(1) .takeWhile { !it.className.startsWith("kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask") } .forEach { println(" at ${it.className.removePrefix("workbench.flows.l03.")}.${it.methodName}") } } io.close() }

alt.title: HandMadeFlowOnJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of HandMadeFlowOn.kt: "flowOn" by hand with an executor and a 64-slot // BlockingQueue. The upstream runs on the executor; the consumer drains the queue on its own thread, // so the consumer's stack holds the draining loop and none of the reader's frames. package workbench.flows.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class HandMadeFlowOnJava { private static final Object END = new Object(); /** Runs upstream on executor, pushes its values through a queue, and delivers them on the caller's thread. */ @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Object> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); executor.execute(() -> { upstream.accept(value -> { try { hatch.put(value); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); try { hatch.put(END); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); for (Object v = hatch.take(); v != END; v = hatch.take()) downstream.accept((T) v); // the drain loop } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ExecutorService io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "io-thread")); Consumer<Consumer<String>> reader = emit -> { emit.accept("flour"); System.out.println("emit flour returned on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); }; flowOn(io, reader, item -> { System.out.println("collected " + item + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); for (StackTraceElement f : Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace()) System.out.println(" at " + f.getClassName().replace("workbench.flows.l03.", "") + "." + f.getMethodName()); }); io.shutdown(); } }

try.expect: The plain flow gives 0, and both myFlowOn(io) and flowOn(io) give 65: 64 in the channel plus the one the collector holds. Every version still receives all 200. The stack shows your collector called from emitAllImpl, and the flow block is not on it. With capacity = 10 your version gives 11. The Java consumer's stack has the loop that empties the queue (flowOn) and main, and none of the reader's frames.

video.title: flowOn(io) builds a wall with a hatch: the reader runs behind it in a second coroutine, a 64-spot shelf lets it get 65 ahead, and the collector and the pantry book never move, which is why withContext around emit is refused; channelFlow lets two cooks share one hatch

sections.h: Several flowOn calls: two walls, three rooms, read from the bottom up
sections.html:
flowOn changes the context of the operators above it, up to the previous flowOn, and nothing below it. With two of them you get two walls and three rooms:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source, publishOn moves what follows,
// and toStream() hands values back to the calling thread through a queue
Flux.range(1, 2)
    .doOnNext(i -> log("emit", i))
    .map(i -> { log("map1", i); return i; })
    .subscribeOn(io)
    .publishOn(cpu)
    .map(i -> { log("map2", i); return i; })
    .toStream()
    .forEach(i -> log("collect", i));
Kotlin
flow { for (i in 1..2) { log("emit", i); emit(i) } }
    .map { log("map1", it); it }
    .flowOn(io)                                // wall 1: everything above runs on io
    .map { log("map2", it); it }
    .flowOn(cpu)                               // wall 2: map2 runs on cpu
    .collect { log("collect", it) }            // the collector's room: main

Coroutine debug mode, a JVM setting (kotlinx.coroutines.debug) that adds each coroutine's number to its thread's name, counts the coroutines for you:

  emit     1   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map1     1   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  emit     2   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map1     2   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map2     1   thread=cpu-thread @coroutine#2
  collect  1   thread=main @coroutine#1
  map2     2   thread=cpu-thread @coroutine#2
  collect  2   thread=main @coroutine#1

Three coroutines, so two channels. The order of lines across threads can change from run to run, but each stage always stays in its room.

Notice the direction. Reactor's publishOn moves what comes after it. Kotlin's flowOn moves what comes before it: it only ever looks up. If you think in Reactor, read flowOn from the bottom up.

Three variants surprise people. First, two flowOn calls with nothing between them fuse into one wall, and the first one, nearest the source, wins. The toString() of flowOf(1, 2, 3).flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) ends with ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO]. (That string is a debug aid, not an API.) A map between them stops the fusion. Second, flowOn(CoroutineName("renamed")) keeps the dispatcher, so it builds no wall; it only puts a new name on the same room. The lines alternate on main like a plain flow, and the upstream's lines show main @renamed#1: the collector's coroutine number with a new name on it. Third, a Job in flowOn is refused as soon as you build the operator, with "Flow context cannot contain job in it."

The common slip comes from looking down instead of up. Someone puts flowOn at the end of a chain and expects it to cover only the slow part:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source, and with no publishOn the stores run on io too
readLines(reader)
    .map(DeliveryLine::parse)
    .doOnNext(pantry::store)         // runs on the io scheduler too
    .subscribeOn(io)
    .blockLast();
Kotlin
readLines(reader)
    .map { parseDeliveryLine(it) }
    .onEach { pantry.store(it) }     // above flowOn, so this runs on io as well
    .flowOn(io)
    .collect()

Here the pantry writes end up behind the wall, on io, which is exactly where the pantry book must never go. Put flowOn directly below the last line that must move: .map { parseDeliveryLine(it) }.flowOn(io).onEach { pantry.store(it) }. That one-line move is the first half of this lesson's lab.

flowOn never moves the collector, wherever you put it. If the collecting side blocks, wrap the terminal call instead, withContext(io) { flow.collect { ... } }, as Flow basics showed.

Read flowOn from the bottom up. It moves what's above it, up to the previous flowOn.

Every room so far had one cook, emitting one plate at a time. Tonight two cooks share the kitchen, and the diner wants plates from both.

Run FlowOnThreadsJava, the Reactor version.

code.title: FlowOnThreads.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.Job import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors fun log(stage: String, v: Any?) = println(" %-8s %-3s thread=%s".format(stage, v, Thread.currentThread().name)) fun main() { // debug mode adds " @coroutine#N" to thread names, so you can count the coroutines System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on") val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "io-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() val cpu = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "cpu-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() runBlocking { println("=== two flowOn calls: two walls, three rooms") flow { for (i in 1..2) { log("emit", i); emit(i) } } .map { log("map1", it); it } .flowOn(io) .map { log("map2", it); it } .flowOn(cpu) .collect { log("collect", it) } println("=== flowOn(CoroutineName): same dispatcher, so no wall") flow { for (i in 1..2) { log("emit", i); emit(i) } } .flowOn(CoroutineName("renamed")) .collect { log("collect", it) } } println("=== adjacent flowOn calls fuse; toString() is a peek under the hood, not an API") val fused = flowOf(1, 2, 3).flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) println(" " + fused.toString().substringAfter(" -> ")) println("=== a Job in flowOn is refused when the operator is built") try { flowOf(1).flowOn(Job()) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println(" " + e.message!!.substringBefore("Had")) } io.close(); cpu.close() }

alt.title: FlowOnThreadsJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowOnThreads.kt with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source (the room behind // the first wall), publishOn moves what follows it (the second wall), and toStream() hands the // values back to the calling thread through a queue (the third room). Reactor moves downstream // with publishOn; Flow's flowOn moves upstream. package workbench.flows.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Scheduler; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class FlowOnThreadsJava { static void log(String stage, Object v) { System.out.printf(" %-8s %-3s thread=%s%n", stage, v, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { Scheduler io = Schedulers.newSingle("io-thread"); Scheduler cpu = Schedulers.newSingle("cpu-thread"); Flux.range(1, 2) .doOnNext(i -> log("emit", i)) .map(i -> { log("map1", i); return i; }) .subscribeOn(io) .publishOn(cpu) .map(i -> { log("map2", i); return i; }) .toStream() .forEach(i -> log("collect", i)); io.dispose(); cpu.dispose(); } }

try.expect: emit and map1 run on io-thread @coroutine#3, map2 on cpu-thread @coroutine#2 and collect on main @coroutine#1: three coroutines and two channels. The fused flow prints ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO]. With CoroutineName, emit and collect alternate on main, and the upstream shows @renamed#1. After the swap, emit and map1 run on cpu-thread and map2 on io-thread. The Reactor version puts emit and map1 on io-thread-2, map2 on cpu-thread-1 and collect on main (Reactor adds a number to each thread name), using publishOn for the second wall.

sections.html:
One cook works the grill and one the oven. Each one is a flow of plates, and the diner wants a single flow that delivers both as they are ready. The obvious code is flow { } with a child coroutine per cook. (launch starts a coroutine that runs alongside the code that started it, from Builders in the coroutines track.)

Java
// Java equivalent: two threads calling one consumer. Nothing stops them calling it at the same time.
Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> grill.forEach(collector::accept));
Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> oven.forEach(collector::accept));
Kotlin
flow {
    coroutineScope {
        launch { grill.collect { emit(it) } }
        launch { oven.collect { emit(it) } }
    }
}

It fails on the first value with an exact, helpful message:

Flow invariant is violated:
		Emission from another coroutine is detected.
		Child of StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@5a8e6209, expected child of BlockingCoroutine{Active}@4b4523f8.
		FlowCollector is not thread-safe and concurrent emissions are prohibited.
		To mitigate this restriction please use 'channelFlow' builder instead of 'flow'

This is the second half of the context check from lesson 2. Two launched children could call emit at the same moment, and the collector would run twice at once. So the inspector refuses any emit from a launched child, and the message names the cure.

channelFlow { } is the builder for this. It's a channel flow like the one flowOn builds, with a 64-spot hatch (Channel.BUFFERED). Its block runs with a ProducerScope, which is both a CoroutineScope you can launch in and a SendChannel you can send to. Its KDoc says the scope "can be used concurrently from different contexts". Several cooks, one hatch, which is the fan-in picture from Channels, select and pipelines:

Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create gives a sink that several threads may call; you complete it yourself
Flux<Plate> both = Flux.create(sink -> {
    Thread g = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> grill.forEach(sink::next));
    Thread o = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> oven.forEach(sink::next));
    Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { join(g); join(o); sink.complete(); });
});
Kotlin
fun bothCooks(grill: Flow<Plate>, oven: Flow<Plate>): Flow<Plate> = channelFlow {
    launch { grill.collect { send(it) } }
    launch { oven.collect { send(it) } }
}

In a run with real threads, on a busy machine, the builder block returned at t=37 ms. The four sends arrived from DefaultDispatcher-worker-1, every collect line printed on main, and the flow completed only at t=133 ms, after both cooks. The block may return early, and the flow still waits for every child. That's structured concurrency, the coroutines track's rule that a parent waits for its children. The cooks are children of the producer coroutine, and its channel closes only when all of them are done, so the collector's loop ends after the last send.

produceIn(scope) is the hatch without the flow around it. It launches a coroutine in your scope that collects the flow, and at once returns the receiving end of the channel, a ReceiveChannel. The collecting starts at the caller's next suspension, whether or not anyone receives. It is hot, running whether anyone takes from it or not: in the demo the upstream started and emitted 1 before anyone called receive. Consume it fully or cancel() it, because the scope waits for that producer coroutine like any other child.

Every hatch in this lesson had the default shelf of 64 spots, and every full shelf made the cook wait. Both are choices, and the next lesson makes them on purpose.

try.title: Let two cooks share one hatch
steps: Run ChannelFlowDemo.kt. Read the error from the flow { } version first.
In the channelFlow part, check three things: the thread of the sent lines, the thread of the collect lines, and when the flow completes compared with the builder block.
In the produceIn part, delete hatch.cancel(). Predict what happens, then run it and stop it with Ctrl+C if it hangs.
Run ChannelFlowDemoJava.

code.title: ChannelFlowDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.channelFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.produceIn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking var t0 = 0L fun at(s: String) = println(" t=%3d %-46s thread=%s".format(System.currentTimeMillis() - t0, s, Thread.currentThread().name)) fun main() = runBlocking { println("=== flow { } with two launched producers") try { flow { coroutineScope { launch { emit("grill-1") } launch { emit("oven-1") } } }.collect { println(" got $it") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println(" " + e.message!!.lines().drop(1).joinToString("\n ").trim()) } println("=== channelFlow: two cooks, one hatch") t0 = System.currentTimeMillis() channelFlow { launch(Dispatchers.IO) { repeat(2) { delay(30); send("grill-$it"); at("sent grill-$it") } } launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(2) { delay(45); send("oven-$it"); at("sent oven-$it") } } at("builder block returns (children still running)") }.collect { at("collect $it") } at("channelFlow completed after both children") println("=== produceIn: a hot channel in your scope") t0 = System.currentTimeMillis() coroutineScope { val hatch = flow { at("upstream started"); for (i in 1..4) { emit(i); at("emitted $i") } } .buffer(1) .produceIn(this) at("produceIn returned a ReceiveChannel") delay(100) at("receiving now: ${hatch.receive()}") hatch.cancel() at("cancelled the channel") } }

alt.title: ChannelFlowDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ChannelFlowDemo.kt: Reactor's Flux.create gives a sink that several threads may // call (it serializes them), much like channelFlow's send. We complete it only after both producer // threads are done, which channelFlow does for you. One difference shows in the output: there is no // hatch here, so the subscriber runs on whichever producer thread calls next. package workbench.flows.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class ChannelFlowDemoJava { static long t0; static void at(String s) { System.out.printf(" t=%3d %-46s thread=%s%n", System.currentTimeMillis() - t0, s, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { t0 = System.currentTimeMillis(); Flux<String> both = Flux.create(sink -> { Thread grill = Thread.ofVirtual().name("grill-cook").start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { sleep(30); sink.next("grill-" + i); at("sent grill-" + i); } }); Thread oven = Thread.ofVirtual().name("oven-cook").start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { sleep(45); sink.next("oven-" + i); at("sent oven-" + i); } }); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { try { grill.join(); oven.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } sink.complete(); // channelFlow completes after its children by itself }); at("create block returns (producers still running)"); }); both.doOnNext(v -> at("collect " + v)).blockLast(); at("flux completed after both producers"); } }

try.expect: The flow { } version fails with "Emission from another coroutine is detected" and the hint to use channelFlow. In the channelFlow part the sends come from a DefaultDispatcher-worker thread, every collect line is on main, and the flow completes only after both cooks, well after the builder block returned. produceIn emits 1 before anyone receives. Without cancel() the program never ends: the producer waits forever on a full one-slot buffer, and the scope waits for it. The Java twin's subscriber runs on the cooks' own threads, because a Reactor sink has no hatch.

compare.title: flowOn by hand: a channel in Kotlin, a BlockingQueue in Java

java.title: HandMadeFlowOnJava.java (abridged)
java.html: // Java equivalent: an executor runs the upstream, a 64-slot queue sits in between static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Object> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); executor.execute(() -> { upstream.accept(value -> put(hatch, value)); // blocks a thread when full put(hatch, END); // a queue can't be closed: send a marker }); for (Object v = hatch.take(); v != END; v = hatch.take()) downstream.accept((T) v); }

kotlin.title: HandMadeFlowOn.kt (abridged)
kotlin.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val hatch = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) { this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) } // suspends when full } // closes the channel when the block ends for (value in hatch) emit(value) } }

compare.note: Both versions have the same three parts: a second worker, a 64-slot hatch, and a loop on the caller's side that empties it. Three things differ, and all of them matter in real programs. A full BlockingQueue blocks a thread, while a full channel suspends a coroutine. A queue can't be closed, so the Java version needs an end marker, while produce closes its channel when its block ends. And the Kotlin version stops cleanly: if the collector fails or stops early, coroutineScope cancels the produce coroutine. In the Java version the reader thread keeps running, blocked on a full queue, until someone interrupts it.

worked.title: Make the delivery import testable in virtual time

steps.say: Say the grocer's website lets the reader fetch only one line per second, so the reader waits before each read. The first version hard-codes the dispatcher. A test with runTest looks fine, but it is slow, and its virtual clock says nothing happened. In a run with three lines on a busy machine, TestTime.kt printed virtual=0 ms, wall=3533 ms: Dispatchers.Default lives outside the test's scheduler, so its delay calls are real.
steps.code: fun slowReader() = flow { repeat(3) { delay(1_000); emit(it) } } // one line per second runTest { slowReader().flowOn(Dispatchers.Default).toList() // virtual=0 ms, wall=3533 ms }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: a hard-coded executor makes the test wait in real time too ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); List<Integer> lines = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> readThreeLinesSlowly(), io).join(); // 3 s of real waiting

steps.say: Inject the dispatcher instead. The real program passes Dispatchers.IO, a test passes something else. Give it a default so callers don't have to care.
steps.code: fun importDelivery( reader: LineReader, pantry: Pantry, io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, // 1. injected, with the real default ): Flow<DeliveryLine> = flow { while (true) emit(reader.readLine() ?: break) } .map { parseDeliveryLine(it) } .flowOn(io) // 2. the wall uses whatever was passed in .onEach { pantry.store(it) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: take the Executor as a constructor argument final class DeliveryImport { private final Executor io; // 1. injected DeliveryImport(Executor io) { this.io = io; } CompletableFuture<List<DeliveryLine>> readAll(LineReader reader) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> parseAll(reader), io); // 2. used here } }

steps.say: For timing tests, pass a test dispatcher that shares the test's scheduler. Its delay calls move the virtual clock, so the same three lines run in milliseconds and the clock reads exactly 3000. flowOn still builds its channel, because a second StandardTestDispatcher is a different dispatcher object.
steps.code: runTest { slowReader().flowOn(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)).toList() // virtual=3000 ms, wall=15 ms }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: a direct executor runs the task on the test thread, with no real pool Executor direct = Runnable::run; List<DeliveryLine> all = new DeliveryImport(direct).readAll(fakeReader).join();

steps.say: For "which side ran where" tests, pass a real executor with one named thread, and record thread names in the fakes. That is how the lab's test checks that readLine ran on test-io and pantry.store on the test thread. Strip the @coroutine#N suffix that debug mode adds when tests run with -ea.
steps.code: val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "test-io") }.asCoroutineDispatcher() fun threadName() = Thread.currentThread().name.substringBefore(" @") val reader = LineReader { readOn += threadName(); lines.removeFirstOrNull() } val pantry = Pantry { storedOn += threadName() } // after collecting: readOn contains only "test-io", storedOn only the test thread

alt.html: ExecutorService io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "test-io")); LineReader reader = () -> { readOn.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); return lines.poll(); }; // after the run: readOn contains only "test-io"

lab.title: Move only the reader, then let two cooks share one hatch
steps: Run the tests. Three of the five fail. Read the messages: one lists the threads that called pantry.store, and two quote "Emission from another coroutine is detected".
Fix importDelivery by moving one line. Reading and parsing must run on io; storing and the collector must not.
Rewrite bothCooks with channelFlow: one launch per cook, and send where the stub calls emit.
Run the tests until all five pass, then run them once more.
hints: flowOn moves the operators above it, up to the previous flowOn. Ask which lines must run on io, and put flowOn directly below the last of them.
Inside channelFlow { }, this is a ProducerScope: a CoroutineScope you can launch in and a SendChannel you can send to. You don't need awaitClose; that's for callbackFlow.
You don't need to close the channel or join the children. channelFlow completes by itself when its block and all its children are done.

The test cooks use delay. runTest's virtual clock covers them, because channelFlow's children inherit the test dispatcher. The merged flow should complete at 390 ms of virtual time, the slower cook's last plate.

drill.title: Write flowOn by hand from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write myFlowOn(dispatcher) with flow { }, coroutineScope, produce and a for loop over the channel. Then answer without running it: where does the block of flow { } run, where does your emit run, and how many emits can return while the collector holds the first value?

answer.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun <T> Flow<T>.myFlowOn(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val hatch = produce(dispatcher, capacity = 64) { // the upstream runs on dispatcher this@myFlowOn.collect { send(it) } } for (value in hatch) emit(value) // our emit runs in the collector's coroutine } } // the upstream's flow { } block runs in the produce coroutine, on dispatcher // 65 emits can return while the collector holds item 1: 64 in the channel, 1 in hand

alt.html: // Java equivalent: an executor for the upstream, a 64-slot queue, a loop on the caller that empties it static <T> void flowOn(ExecutorService executor, Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Object> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); executor.execute(() -> { upstream.accept(value -> put(hatch, value)); put(hatch, END); }); for (Object v = hatch.take(); v != END; v = hatch.take()) downstream.accept((T) v); }

recap: The collector runs inside emit, so emit must run in the collector's context. withContext around emit would drag the collector onto another thread, and flow { } refuses it.
When the dispatcher changes, flowOn runs the upstream in a second coroutine and puts a channel between the two halves, 64 slots by default: a wall with a hatch. The producer can get 65 emits ahead.

flowOn moves only the operators above it, up to the previous flowOn. Two calls make two walls and three rooms; two adjacent calls fuse, and the first one wins. With the same dispatcher, as in flowOn(CoroutineName(...)), there is no channel.
To emit from several coroutines, use channelFlow: send is safe from any child, and the flow completes after every child. produceIn hands you the channel itself, hot, in your scope.
In tests, inject the dispatcher that flowOn uses. flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) inside runTest runs on the real clock.
The limit: every hatch here had the default 64 spots and made the producer wait when full. Choosing the size, and what to drop instead of waiting, is the next lesson.

explain.prompt: A friend moved a blocking delivery-note reader with withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(line) }, got "Flow invariant is violated", and asks why Kotlin forbids something so obvious. Explain it, and say what flowOn does instead.
explain.answer: In a flow, emit isn't a hand-off. It's a direct call into the collector, so the collector's code runs inside emit. If emit ran inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO), our collector, the part that writes in the pantry book, would suddenly run on an IO thread it never asked for, next to code that isn't thread-safe. flow { } checks every emit and refuses that. flowOn solves it by breaking the call chain. When the dispatcher changes, it starts a second coroutine on IO that runs everything above flowOn and sends each value into a channel with 64 slots, and on our side a loop takes values out and calls our collector in its own coroutine. So the reader runs on IO, can get up to 65 values ahead, and the collector stays exactly where it was. It only moves what's above it, so we put it right under the blocking read.

deeper.html:
Some details of flowOn only show up in real programs.

It can lose values in flight on cancellation. Its KDoc says that "flows operating across different dispatchers might lose some in-flight elements when cancelled", and that the operator "ensures that downstream flow does not resume on cancellation even if the element was already emitted by the upstream flow". For the delivery import that means the reader may have read lines that never reached the pantry book. If that matters, track what was stored, not what was read.

Whether a channel appears depends on dispatcher objects, not threads. With a collector already on Dispatchers.IO, flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) stays sequential, with no channel. With a collector on Dispatchers.Default, flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) creates one, even though the two dispatchers share threads, because they are different objects.

Stability in 1.11.0: flowOn, channelFlow, callbackFlow and produceIn compile with no opt-in. CoroutineScope.produce, which the hand-built myFlowOn uses, is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi. Use the library's operators in real code and keep myFlowOn as the model in your head.

callbackFlow, from lesson 9 of the coroutines track, is a subclass of the same channelFlow builder. The difference is one check: if its block returns while the channel is still open, it throws an IllegalStateException telling you to call awaitClose { ... } at the end. Lesson 8 of this track wraps a listener API with it.

buffer() is the same machine as flowOn without the context change, and neighbouring channel operators fuse into one channel. Lesson 4 of this track takes that apart, using toString() as a peek under the hood.
